1:
The speech opens in temper, and every witness says so. Gill lists what Zophar disregards in order to begin — the distressed condition Job was in, his earnest request for pity, the confession of faith he had just made, and his advice that they cease persecuting him — and says he starts up regardless of all of it, with as much heat and passion, wrath and anger as ever, still representing Job as a wicked man and a hypocrite. Ellicott marks the escalation in manner as well as matter, that he retorts with yet greater vehemence than before and assumes a more ornate and elaborate style while reiterating the same burden of the speedy doom of the wicked. Henry describes the same entry more closely: being resolved to condemn Job for a bad man, Zophar was displeased that he talked so like a good man, broke in upon him and began abruptly, taking no notice of anything said to move their pity or to evidence his integrity and fastening instead on the reproof at the close. Clarke is the harshest, calling Zophar the most inveterate of them all and saying that we really must cease to call these men friends, since he sets no bounds to his invective and outrages every rule of charity.

Whether the second verse can be construed at all is the chapter's first technical dispute. Keil and Delitzsch report that all modern expositors take it as an apology for the opposition that follows and that the majority read the preposition as elliptical, with Ewald defending its standing without addition; and then they refuse the result, holding that in spite of this the verse furnishes no meaning that can be accepted, and rejecting the sense of a disturbance of mind proposed by Schultens as too remote from the usage of Hebrew. The others render it without visible difficulty. Clarke reports Good's version, which asks whither the speaker's tumult would transport him and how far his agitation within, and remarks drily that this is all the modesty that appears in the discourse; he renders the second clause as meaning that there is sensibility in him and his feelings provoke him to reply. Ellicott glosses it simply as the eagerness that is in him, his spirit stirred and impelling him to answer, and Wesley reads it as haste, that he speaks sooner than he intended and possibly interrupted Job in the middle of his discourse.
3:
What the reproach was, and whether the answer is reason or passion, divides the rest. Gill takes the check to be Job's warning that they should beware of the sword, and adds that some understand Zophar to be claiming a divine oracle of the kind Eliphaz had alleged earlier in the dispute, so that being divinely furnished he thought it his duty to deliver it. Clarke offers two possibilities, that Zophar is quoting Job's own words or referring to the complaint that they had reproached him ten times over, and concludes that he assumes his old ground and retracts nothing, being determined to believe his judgment infallible. Ellicott renders it as a reproof that puts him to shame and reads the following clause literally, that out of his understanding his spirit answers him, so that he professes an impulse within which he cannot but obey. On whether the profession is true the witnesses part. Wesley takes him at his word, that he speaks not from passion but from certain knowledge. Henry will not, observing that the abundance of the heart is what the mouth speaks while Zophar fathers the instigation on the spirit of his understanding, and adding that men often mistake the dictates of their passion for the dictates of their reason and therefore think they do well to be angry.

Gregory reads the whole opening differently, as a mind shaken rather than a temper roused. Taking the words as the confusion of one who sees the terribleness of the last Judgment, he says the mind spreads itself wider in its range of thought the more it considers how dreadful is the thing that threatens it, and is transported diverse ways when it weighs by turns the evil it has done and the good it has left undone. He is nevertheless clear about where the friends went wrong: though instructed by long acquaintance with Job's life to know how to live well, they were uninstructed in forming an exact estimate of God's judgments and would not believe that any of the righteous could be susceptible of ills here below, so that seeing him scourged they imagined a holy man to be wicked and slipped into upbraiding him, though under the guise of a kind of respect. Henry adds the maxim the exchange illustrates, that the best counsel is too often ill taken from an antagonist, and observes that Job's friends had spirits too high to deal with a man in his low condition.
4:
The appeal to antiquity is read two ways. Gill takes the phrase as from eternity or from the beginning of time and makes it a taunt, that if Job is the knowing man he pretends to be he must know a maxim so old; and he adds the obvious qualification, that Job could not have known it from so early, being neither the first man born nor made before the hills but comparatively of yesterday. Clarke reads the second clause literally as since Adam was placed on the earth, that is since the fall, and turns the verse back on the speaker: Job had lately been expressing confidence about a general judgment, and such is Zophar's character that he has little reason to anticipate that day with any joy.

The maxim itself is stated, and one witness refuses it. Ellicott summarises the claim exactly, that the destruction of the wicked is affirmed to be not only certain but speedy. Gill traces how the friends arrived at it, that they set out with the notion that the wicked never prospered at all and, being beaten out of that, now concede a short prosperity instead; and then he declines to grant even the reduced version, saying it may be true in many instances but is not invariable and without exception the case. He notes that the Hebrew phrase is literally from near, so that the triumph began only a little while ago, and that the Targum paraphrases it as quickly ended.

The height from which the fall is measured draws two quite different illustrations. Gill reaches for the ambitions of empire, the Assyrian monarch who would ascend into heaven and exalt his throne above the stars of God, and the tree whose height reached to heaven by which the greatness of Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom was figured. Clarke keeps to the first man, supposing the reference to be to the original state of Adam, created in the image of God and fallen by his own sin into wretchedness, misery, death and destruction. Wesley reduces it to its plainest sense, advancement to great dignity and authority.

The comparison in the seventh verse is the harshest in the speech, and the commentators respond in kind. Gill presses the figure to its end, that the man perishes in his own corruption as inevitably as dung, which is never returned to its place, and supports it from ancient usage, that dead bodies were reckoned as dung and that the Arabians buried even their kings in dunghills. Clarke hears a doctrine underneath the insult and objects to it, suspecting that Zophar hints his disbelief in the resurrection of the body which Job had so solemnly asserted in the preceding chapter, or else held what some in his own day hold, that the wicked are annihilated and the bodies of the righteous only raised — a doctrine he says he knows no scripture to confirm. Gill, who takes the perishing to reach the soul in eternity as well as the body in the grave, is by implication on the other side of that question. Clarke closes on the manner rather than the matter, calling it a speech that partakes as much of the malevolence as of the asperity of Zophar's spirit.
8:
The figure of the dream is taken two ways. Gill offers both: either a dream that is forgotten, as Nebuchadnezzar's was, and cannot be recovered at all, or the substance of a dream which, though remembered, was never anything but illusion, as a hungry man dreams he eats and wakes empty and not at all refreshed. Clarke hears the same verse as a continued denial of what Job had just asserted, that instead of rising again from corruption with a new body his flesh shall rot and his spirit be dissipated like a vapour, so that nothing remains but the bare impression that such a creature once existed. Gill keeps the tenth verse to this world, the eye that saw him busy in the affairs of life seeing him so no more.

The next verse is the most variously rendered in the chapter, and Clarke says so outright. The received reading has the man's children seeking to please the poor, which Gill explains as their courting after his death the good will of those he had oppressed, so as to escape reproach or revenge or a suit before the magistrate, though he notes that Jarchi renders it otherwise. Clarke takes the same words to mean that the children are reduced to the lowest degree of want, obliged to become servants to the poor, which he calls the most abject poverty there is, and cites the curse upon Ham for a servant of servants; he then gives Good's quite different version, that the man's branches shall be involved in his iniquity, so that the children suffer on his account, and Calmet's third, that his own hands shall render to himself the evil he did to others. Ellicott adds a fourth, that the clause may be rendered the other way round, so that the poor oppress his children. Gill supplies the doctrine the verse is made to carry, that children are often visited in wrath for their parents' sins, especially when they tread in their steps.

What his bones are full of divides the witnesses four ways, and the division is lexical rather than doctrinal. Gill takes it literally of youthful sin and its bodily aftermath, listing the sins the young age is addicted to and finding their effect in the rottenness of flesh and putrefaction of bone, while noting that some read the word as secret sins. Clarke prefers that second sense and names its supporters, holding that the word may be rendered his hidden things so that secret vices bring down his strength to the dust, with Rosenmuller and several German critics and Good all contending for it; and he reports that the Syriac, the Arabic and the Targum read the line quite differently, that his bones are full of marrow. Ellicott takes the word for neither sin nor secrecy but for youthful vigour, so that the sense is that a man in the full vigour of life shall yet lie down with it in the dust. Wesley reads the bones as the whole body, even its strongest parts, and the sin as the punishment of it. Henry, who is sorting the speech into heads, simply files the clause under the lusts of the flesh, those being the sins to which that age is most tempted.
12:
What the sweetness stands for is disputed before the figure is even unfolded. Gill judges from the context that a particular sin is meant, covetousness or the getting of riches unlawfully, and reports Broughton rendering the word as wrong, though he allows it may be applied to sin in general, which is sweet to a man whose taste is unchanged and who calls bitter sweet. Clarke refers it instead to the secret sins of the preceding verse. Henry files it under the forbidden pleasures of sense, the sins of youth again. Ellicott suspects a target rather than a category: Zophar draws the wicked man after the pattern of a gourmand, and if that was meant to apply to Job it was a fresh instance of heartless cruelty and of an entire want of discernment of character, as well as of unfitness for the office of judge he was so ready to assume; the reproach, he thinks, may be an inordinate love of riches extracted from the bare fact that Job had been wealthy.

The hiding under the tongue is read as gluttony, as obstinacy and as concealment. Wesley gives the plainest picture, an epicure with a sweet morsel which he keeps and rolls about his mouth so as to enjoy the pleasure of it the longer. Clarke sets out the whole allegory at once, a man who takes poison instead of wholesome food and is so delighted by the taste that he will scarcely let it down, until on swallowing it turns to gall within him. Henry offers two senses and does not choose: keeping it in the mouth may denote obstinate persistence, since he spares what he should kill and mortify, and also the re-acting of the sin by revolving it and remembering it with pleasure; or the hiding may denote a hypocrite's industrious concealment of his beloved lust, so as to save the credit of his profession — though he adds that the one who knows what is in the heart knows what is under the tongue too. Gill reads the sparing not as eating little but as valuing much, since the man does not spit it out as loathsome but retains it, sparing it as Saul spared Agag and as a man spares an only son, sin being a wicked man's own child and therefore dear to him.

The turn from sweet to bitter is where the allegory pays out. Gill presses the comparison of sin to bread, the thing a sinner lives in and lives upon and is nourished by, but bread of deceit that proves to be ashes and gravel stones, promising pleasure, profit, liberty and impunity and being all the reverse; and he keeps the physical figure exact, that meat turns in a man's stomach when it will not digest, so that instead of being pleasant it distresses him. Wesley grades the bitterness in three steps, that gall is most bitter, that the gall of serpents is full of poison, and that the poison of asps is the most dangerous of all and within a few hours kills without remedy. Keil and Delitzsch, giving their own rendering of this run of verses, notice what the imagery is playing against and reach outside Scripture for it, the golden age of which the poets sang, when rivers of milk and rivers of nectar ran — the streams of honey and cream that this man is told he shall never see.
15:
The swallowing and the vomiting are kept strictly to the figure. Gill notes that the riches swallowed are not his own but another's, spoiled from him and devoured as eagerly as a hungry man swallows food, and that once they are down the man thinks them as safe as meat in his belly and never dreams of refunding them. Clarke supplies the physiology the image depends on, that most ordinary poisons occasion nausea and violent vomiting, nature striving to eject what it knows will be its bane if retained.

Whether the poison is the sin or the punishment is a flat contradiction between two of the witnesses. Gill argues from the tense that it cannot be the sin, since that would have required a past or present form, as though the wickedness had been sucked in like milk from the breast; it is the punishment instead, and he observes that execution by the poison of asps was a penalty some peoples actually inflicted on malefactors. Clarke reads it the other way round without qualification: that delicious morsel, the secret and easily besetting sin, acts on the life of the soul exactly as the poison of an asp acts on the body. Both then reach for the same naturalist. Gill cites Pliny for the placing of the venom, whether in the teeth or as a yellow liquor in the gums, and repeats his account of the asps in copulation; Clarke cites him for the older belief that the poison lay in the gall, which was thought to be exuded when the creature was enraged, since the bite was held harmless when it was not, and notes that the same author ranks the gall of horses among the poisons, so that the idea was current in Italy as well as in Arabia.

The rivers of honey and butter draw the chapter's widest reading. Gill takes the denial of water first, since poison excites thirst, and recalls the rich man who asked for a drop to cool his tongue, though he thinks plenty of good things is the likelier sense. Clarke relays Good's account of the image, that honey and butter are the natural yield of a rich well-watered pasturage, a perpetual banquet of grass to cattle and of nectar to bees, and so the most luscious luxuries of pastoral life, especially before the means of obtaining sugar were discovered; the phrase, he thinks, was proverbial for a very high degree of temporal prosperity. He then sets beside it a shelf of classical parallels — Pindar comparing his own song to milk and honey for smoothness, Virgil wishing honey from the oaks of a friend's estate, Ovid describing the golden age with floods of milk and nectar, and Horace with honeyed streams from hollow oaks. Ellicott draws a quieter but more consequential inference from the same words: the language might suggest a writer familiar with the promise made of Canaan, except that the phrase is not precisely identical, which may rather show a community of proverbial speech, and that the land flowing with milk and honey was an expression already in use and not one original with the Pentateuch. Wesley states the loss plainly, that he shall not enjoy the abundant satisfaction which good men have through God's blessing.
18:
The eighteenth verse is the most disputed line in the chapter, and Clarke breaks off to say so. He prefers a reading he finds in the Arabic and supported by the Syriac and nearer the Hebrew than the received version, that the man shall return to labour but shall not eat, toiling without being permitted to enjoy the fruit of it; he then gives Good's rendering, which makes a dearth his recompense so that he tastes nothing at all, and explains how it is reached from two Arabic words, one for eating and one for a barren year. Against both he sets Houbigant, who has the man restore what he gained by labour and not consume it, his merchandise abundant and unenjoyed — at which point Clarke exclaims at how the doctors disagree, and adds that Coverdale gives a good sense, that he shall labour and have nothing to eat and make great travail for riches he will not enjoy. Keil and Delitzsch object on syntax rather than lexicon, refusing the translation that has him giving back what he gained without swallowing it, and rejecting every attempt to attach the last phrase to the first, whether by making it property that is to be restored or the property of another, as Hahn does; such readings, they say, run against the relative independence of the separate lines of a verse which this poet almost always preserves. Ellicott allows the latter part is probably right but offers his own alternative, that according to the substance he has gotten he shall not rejoice. Gill and Wesley leave the construction alone and take the plain sense, Gill noting that the verse explains in words what vomiting had expressed in figure, and Wesley that the man shall be forced to part with his estate to make compensation for his wrongs.

The charge in the next verse is read as darkly as the words allow, and then rebutted. Gill will not let it be softened into the desertion of former dependents, since the man was never their favourer, and cites the reading that he does not leave the poor until he has crushed them, alongside Broughton's version that he oppresses and leaves poor. Clarke renders it more literally still as the breaking in pieces of the forsaken of the poor, and supplies a scene for it: the poor have fled from famine and left their children behind, and this hard-hearted wretch, whom Zophar means to be Job all the while, has suffered them to perish when he might have saved them alive; and the house violently taken away he reads as a house thrown down and not rebuilt, a family left to become extinct that might have been preserved. Ellicott answers the accusation instead of expounding it, saying flatly that for these insinuations there was not a vestige of ground and that Job formally rebuts them later in the book.

The last verse turns from the man's deeds to his interior, and the question is whether the restlessness is his sin or his sentence. Gill canvasses three senses, happiness in his children, satisfaction in his substance, and the restless craving after more which would make the want of quiet his sin rather than his punishment, and then decides for punishment, that he has no quiet in his conscience because of the way his riches were got. Clarke takes the word rendered belly in its wider scriptural sense of the whole trunk and therefore of the thoughts, purposes and inclinations seated there, and makes the verse mean that the man shall never be satisfied but shall have an endless desire after secular good. Ellicott turns the clause into the cause rather than the effect, that because he knew no quietness within him he shall save nothing of what he desires. Wesley reduces it to no peace in his mind, and the forfeiting of every desirable thing.
21:
The twenty-first verse is short enough to be turned inside out, and it is. Gill offers three readings: that nothing is left in his belly, all being cast up; that the clause describes either his profuseness or his niggardliness, keeping so mean a table that not a crumb falls from it; or that the words mean there shall be none left for his substance, so that he leaves no children and has no heirs. Ellicott reverses the sentence entirely, making it say that there was nothing left which he did not devour, and that therefore his prosperity shall not endure. Clarke quotes Coverdale to the same effect, that he devoured so greedily that he left nothing behind. Wesley reads the ending as a social fact, that his ruin being publicly known none of his kindred will trouble themselves about the relics of his estate.

The paradox of the next verse is admired even by those who differ about it. Clarke calls it a fine saying which few menders of the text have been able to improve, and says it is literally true of every great, rich, wicked man, who has no God and is tormented by anxieties in the midst of his portion. Gill lists the ways fulness turns to straitness — fear of losing what he has, so that his abundance will not let him sleep; a narrowness of spirit that will not let him eat of the fruit of his own labours; or a dread of coming to want — before preferring the sharpest, that in the height of prosperity he is suddenly dispossessed of everything, as Nebuchadnezzar was. Keil and Delitzsch read the clause about filling as introducing what follows, that in order to fill a belly which is insatiable God will send forth his glowing wrath and rain it upon the man's very flesh. Who the hands are that fall on him is disputed: Ellicott reads them as the hands of the miserable, coming upon him in retaliation, and mentions but doubts a second sense in which every blow that can make a man wretched shall reach him; Wesley makes them the hands of men as wicked as himself, so that his wickedness is punished by his own kind.

What the eating alludes to divides the chapter's two boldest readings. Clarke argues at length for the wilderness, finding a plain allusion to the lustings of Israel in the desert, where God showered down quails and showered down his wrath while the flesh was yet in their mouth; he supports it with a rendering from the bishop of Killala which takes the word translated quietness in the earlier verse as a quail, and then sets four of these verses side by side with the narrative of the manna and the quails and with the psalm that retells it. Henry and Wesley hear a much more local and crueller allusion. Wesley glosses the word about eating with the remark that the wrath fell so upon Job's own sons, and Henry suggests outright that Zophar may here be reflecting on the death of Job's children while they were eating and drinking. Henry otherwise dwells on the weight of the language, that every word speaks terror, since it is not only God's justice but his wrath, and the fury of that wrath, cast with force and rained in abundance like the fire and brimstone upon Sodom; and he adds that the blow falls when the man is secure and easy, as ruin came upon the old world and upon Sodom in the depth of their security and the height of their sensuality.
24:
The flight from one weapon into another is read as a single designed movement. Keil and Delitzsch arrange the two verbs as a conditional clause and take that to be the relation the poet intended: if he flees the iron weapon, the deadly thing in the thick of the fight, he succumbs by and by to what destroys at a distance, the brazen bow piercing him through, so that the flight of a disheartened man is a punishment completed by the arrow that overtakes him in it. Clarke reaches the same sense and quotes Coverdale for it, that if he flee the iron weapon he shall be shot with the steel bow, concluding that he shall most certainly perish since all kinds of death await him. Ellicott states it as a rule, that if he escaped one mischance another should overtake him. Gill reads the weapon as the sword of God, on Bar Tzemach's authority, and takes the flight itself as evidence, since it shows guilt in the conscience and a sense of danger, while there is no fleeing from the presence of God at all.

Where the arrow is drawn from is a small disagreement with a visible consequence. Gill reports Broughton taking it of the quiver and prefers the other, that it is drawn out of the man's body in the hope of curing the wound, and to no purpose. Clarke reads the whole verse as archery in sequence, the arrow taken from the sheaf, discharged from the bow, piercing the vitals and passing through, and again quotes Coverdale, that it shall go out at his back. Wesley follows the clause to the particular organ named and draws the inference, that the mention of the gall shows the wound to have been deep and deadly, and that the terrors are the terrors of death because the man perceived it was incurable. Ellicott takes the terrors as cumulative, that even after escaping a second and a third calamity they remain upon him — and then steps outside the exposition to judge it, saying that all of this was perfectly true in a sense and even a truism, but utterly false in its application to Job himself.

The secret places are the last thing disputed, and there are three answers. Gill gives all of them: the places of concealment where the man promises himself safety and finds calamity instead; the store of everlasting wrath laid up among God's own treasures of vengeance; or, as Ben Gersom takes it and as Broughton renders the phrase, his store of secret sins, which however privately committed shall be brought into judgment. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both take the word of hoarded goods rather than hiding places, Ellicott reading that every kind of disaster is laid up for his secret treasures, and Keil and Delitzsch adding the contrast that gives the clause its edge, that where one Psalm calls God's store of earthly goods for men a treasured thing, here the stores a man lays up for himself are so called, and total darkness is decreed against them because they were gathered covetously and without regard to the hand that gives. Wesley keeps the hiding-place sense and presses it, that even where he confidently hopes to hide from all evil God shall find him out. On the fire, all agree it is not kindled by man, and Clarke alone names a precedent, suspecting an allusion to the fire that fell on Korah and his company, which he thinks explains the closing threat against whoever is left in the man's tent.
27:
Who or what the heaven is that reveals him is answered three ways by one witness. Gill offers God himself, the maker and possessor of heaven who sees what is most secret; or the angels of heaven, as the Targum takes it, who will gather out of Christ's kingdom all that offend; or the judgments that descend from heaven and are owing to it, instancing the drowning of the old world when its windows were opened, the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, and destruction by thunder and lightning. Wesley makes it God as a swift witness by extraordinary judgments and adds a pointed aside, that Zophar is still reflecting on Job's case and the fire that fell from heaven upon his flocks; and he takes the answering clause as a conspiracy of all creatures, since if the God of heaven and earth be a man's enemy neither will show him any kindness. Ellicott says the same in one sentence, that all nature combines to bring about a ruin which is in fact decreed by God, and then closes the speech with an observation about the speaker rather than the doctrine: here we take leave of Zophar, who does not reply again, having exhausted himself for all his opening boast about the thoughts that compelled him to answer.

The dissolving of the house draws one lexical note and one long argument. Gill takes the increase for either his children or his substance, and reports from Kimchi a reading that makes it the walls, since a dilapidation can be expressed as a pouring down of stones, so that the house itself falls and flows away. Wesley keeps it to the estate, lost and flowing off like water swiftly and strongly, so as to return no more. Clarke hears in it a third thing altogether, a further allusion to the punishment of the company of Korah, who perished not alone but with their houses and their goods, and he presses the inference: these examples were all in point on the ground Zophar had taken, and such well-attested facts would not have been passed over by him had he known the record of them — which, since he alludes to them and quotes the very circumstances, Clarke thinks more than probable.
29:
That inference is the chapter's largest claim, and Clarke states it openly at the close. Following Dr. Stock, bishop of Killala, who had read the word for quietness in the earlier verse as a quail and who Clarke says has been most unmeritedly ridiculed for it, he holds that the poet is doing what Hebrew poets are known to do, adorning his composition with allusions to facts in his own people's history; and the bishop's point, which Clarke says escaped all the interpreters, is that this fixes the date of the poem, proving it composed after the transgression of Israel at the place of the graves of lust. Clarke claims to have strengthened the reasoning by adding the manna and the rebellion of Korah to the quails, and draws the conclusion without hedging: it is a proof that the Book of Job is not so old as the Pentateuch, much less older, as some have endeavoured to prove. Ellicott, earlier in the same chapter, had reasoned from the opposite end of the same kind of evidence, observing that the language about brooks of honey and butter is not precisely identical with the promise made of Canaan and may therefore show a community of proverbial speech rather than dependence, so that the phrase need not have originated with the Pentateuch at all. Neither cites the other, and the chapter leaves the question where they leave it.

The closing verse is read for the word portion. Gill draws the contrast that governs the whole speech, that a wicked man does indeed have his portion from God, but his portion is not God himself, as a good man's is; it is at most in this life and afterwards among devils and damned spirits. Wesley stops on the second noun, which he says is called the heritage to denote its stability, being as firm as an inheritance to the right heir, and set deliberately against the inheritance the man had got by fraud and violence. Clarke reads the verse as the application of his own historical parallels, that as God dealt with the murmuring Israelites and the rebellious sons of Korah, so he will deal with those who murmur against the dispensations of providence, who instead of an earthly portion shall have fire to scorch them and earth to swallow them up.
